title: The shape of things
subtitle: Build surfaces from points and triangles.

lessons.title: A vocabulary of shapes
body: Primitives are ready-made shapes such as boxes, spheres, cylinders, and toruses. Their constructor arguments define dimensions and subdivisions.

A torus is a ring: its first argument is the main radius, and the second is the tube radius. The remaining arguments control how finely the ring is divided. Start with primitives before reaching for an imported 3D model.
lessons.task: Replace the box with new THREE.TorusGeometry(1, 0.3, 16, 64).
lessons.hint: Keep the geometry variable and change its constructor.

quiz.question: What is a torus?
quiz.explanation: A torus is the familiar doughnut or ring shape.

lessons.title: Smoothness has a cost
body: Curved surfaces are approximated by flat triangles. More subdivisions can make the silhouette smoother, but they also require more geometry processing and memory.

This sphere starts with only 6 width segments. Increase that count and inspect the silhouette, especially near the edges. Material shading can smooth the light across a surface, but it cannot round a coarse silhouette.
lessons.hint: The widthSegments variable is passed as SphereGeometry’s second argument.

quiz.question: What improves when you add segments to a sphere?
quiz.explanation: More triangles approximate the curved outline more closely.

lessons.title: See the hidden triangles
body: The renderer ultimately draws triangles. Even the faces of a box, which look square, are usually split into pairs of triangles.

Wireframe mode draws triangle edges instead of filled surfaces. It is useful for inspecting geometry density and seeing why some shapes cost more to draw than others. Orbit around this knot to inspect how its surface is constructed.
lessons.hint: Change false to true on the final line.

quiz.question: A typical mesh surface is built from…
quiz.explanation: Triangles are the basic surface primitive used by this WebGL renderer.

lessons.title: Shape your first triangle
body: A vertex is a point used to define geometry. BufferGeometry stores vertex data in typed arrays called attributes. The position attribute uses three numbers per vertex: X, Y, Z.

This triangle has three vertices. Raise the top vertex by changing its Y coordinate. After changing an existing attribute, mark it needsUpdate so the new data reaches the GPU. Recompute normals when a deformation changes how a lit surface should face.
lessons.task: Set the top vertex’s Y coordinate to 2.
lessons.hint: Change positions.setY(2, 1) to positions.setY(2, 2). The first argument is the vertex index.

quiz.question: What does the 3 in Float32BufferAttribute(data, 3) mean?
quiz.explanation: Each position uses three components: x, y, and z.

lessons.title: Which way does a surface face?
body: A normal is a direction perpendicular to a surface. Lighting uses normals to decide how strongly a surface faces a light. MeshNormalMaterial lets you inspect these directions as colors.

Smooth shading blends vertex normals across a face; flat shading gives each triangle a distinct face normal. Neither changes the silhouette. Toggle flat shading on this low-detail sphere and notice its faceted look.
lessons.hint: The material is marked needsUpdate afterward so its shader can be rebuilt.

quiz.question: Does smooth shading add triangles?
quiz.explanation: Shading changes the appearance of the existing surface, not its geometry.
